newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection continues in Florida tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection continues in Florida tobacco case.

text.p: Jury selection continued Tuesday in the trial of a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, with potential jurors being asked about the novel "Runaway Jury" by best-selling author John Grisham.

The issue of Grisham's book -- a story of jury manipulation at a tobacco trial that has haunted cigarette makers fighting numerous lawsuits in Florida -- arose on the second day of the trial of Raulerson vs R.J. Reynolds, in which the sister of a smoker who died of lung cancer has accused the tobacco company of peddling a deadly product.
Several prospective jurors said they had read or were reading the book.

In "Runaway Jury," a tobacco industry operative commissions a burglary and other crimes as part of a juror-tampering campaign. The novel reflects the concerns of anti-tobacco lawyers worried about real-life jury tampering -- which in turn angers the lawyers representing the tobacco companies.
"You understand that book is fantasy, right?" Paul Crist, a lawyer for Reynolds, asked one member of the jury pool.
To the entire group of 25 prospective jurors, he said, "Will you -- each one of you -- commit to me you'll have no contact with the lawyers?"
Jury selection began Monday and was expected to take several days. As of midday Tuesday, one member of the jury pool had been dismissed and none had been seated.
Lawyers asked the prospective jurors questions about addiction and their beliefs about personal and corporate responsibility.

Various jurors admitted to being addicted to exercise, the Internet, tea and caffeine. Asked whether smoking is like being addicted to heroin, one potential juror said, "For some people, it probably is."

The lawsuit alleges that Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp and the second-largest U.S. cigarette maker, deceived the public with misleading ads. Reynolds' attorneys have contended that the late Jean Connor, who died of cancer in 1995 at age 49, and whose sister Dana Raulerson brought the case, had made an informed decision to smoke.
Crist characterized the trial as being "about Jean Connor and the decisions she made during her lifetime."
Six jurors and three alternates will be selected for a trial expected to last two to three weeks.
